# Diagnostics Ask Several Different Questions

For the Cox model

$$
h(t\mid x)=h_0(t)\exp(x^\mathsf{T}\beta),
$$

the proportional-hazards (PH) assumption says each modeled coefficient is
constant over follow-up. That is only one part of model adequacy. A responsible
diagnostic analysis separately asks whether:

1. covariate effects change with time;
2. continuous covariates have appropriate functional forms;
3. individual subjects or risk sets dominate the fit;
4. censoring, entry, dependence, and competing-event handling match the design;
5. predictions are calibrated and useful for the intended population.

No single residual plot or global $p$-value answers all five questions. A model
can satisfy PH yet have severe nonlinearity or informative censoring, and it can
fail PH while still yielding useful time-specific predictions after revision.

# Schoenfeld Residuals Target Proportionality

At an event time $t_d$, let subject $i(d)$ experience the event and define the
risk-score-weighted covariate mean

$$
\bar x(\hat\beta,t_d)=
\frac{\sum_{j\in R(t_d)}x_j\exp(x_j^\mathsf{T}\hat\beta)}
{\sum_{j\in R(t_d)}\exp(x_j^\mathsf{T}\hat\beta)}.
$$

The Schoenfeld residual vector is

$$
\boxed{r_d=x_{i(d)}-\bar x(\hat\beta,t_d).}
$$

It compares the covariates of the subject who failed with the weighted average
among subjects who could have failed then. There is one residual vector per
event time, not one ordinary residual per censored subject. Its components are
also contributions to the partial-likelihood score.

Under a correctly specified PH effect, appropriately scaled Schoenfeld residuals
should fluctuate around a horizontal pattern when plotted against a chosen
function of time. A smooth trend estimates how the coefficient may depart from
its fitted constant. Grambsch and Therneau's test formalizes this as a score test
for association between scaled residuals and transformed event time.

## Read the plot and the test together

A practical display includes the scaled residuals, a smooth estimate of
$\beta_j(t)$, and an uncertainty band. The key questions are:

- Is the smooth approximately horizontal?
- Is the departure large enough to change scientific interpretation?
- Is the pattern localized to a sparse tail with few subjects at risk?
- Does it persist under plausible time transformations and influential-unit
  checks?

Software may test transformed time such as Kaplan--Meier, rank, or identity
time. Different transformations emphasize different alternatives. A small
$p$-value says the chosen constant-effect model is inconsistent with the tested
time pattern; it does not specify the best replacement. A large $p$-value may
reflect low power, few events, or cancellation of nonmonotone departures.

# What Nonproportional Hazards Mean

Suppose the more general data-generating model is

$$
h(t\mid x)=h_0(t)\exp\{x^\mathsf{T}\beta(t)\}.
$$

For covariate $x_j$, $\exp\{\beta_j(t)\}$ is a time-specific hazard ratio. A
constant Cox fit compresses that curve into a weighted average whose weights
depend on event times, risk sets, censoring, and other covariates. The estimate
is therefore not a universal average biological effect.

Nonproportionality can arise from several mechanisms:

- a treatment benefit wanes or is delayed;
- a continuous covariate was modeled linearly when its effect is nonlinear;
- an omitted interaction changes the effect across subgroups whose risk-set
  composition changes over time;
- unmodeled frailty selectively removes high-risk subjects from the risk set;
- the endpoint combines event types with different covariate relationships; or
- measurement or treatment status changes during follow-up.

Diagnostics reveal tension with the working model, but scientific context is
needed to distinguish these mechanisms.

# Remedies Must Match the Scientific Target

| Pattern or goal | Possible model revision | Interpretation |
|---|---|---|
| Nuisance categorical variable violates PH | Stratify on that variable | Separate baseline hazards; no coefficient for the stratifier |
| Effect changes smoothly over time | Include $x_jg(t)$ or estimate $\beta_j(t)$ | Report hazard ratios at prespecified times or as a curve |
| Effect differs before and after a meaningful time | Piecewise coefficient with a prespecified cut point | Separate interval-specific hazard ratios |
| Continuous covariate is nonlinear | Restricted cubic spline or justified transformation | Effect depends on covariate value, not necessarily time |
| Absolute prognosis is the target | Estimate and validate survival or cumulative incidence at relevant times | Emphasize calibrated risks, not only relative hazards |
| PH is scientifically implausible | Consider an accelerated failure-time, additive-hazards, or flexible parametric model | The estimand and coefficient scale change |

Choosing a cut point after inspecting the same residual plot understates
uncertainty. Prefer prespecified structure or flexible functions with honest
uncertainty and validation. If the scientific question concerns a marginal
survival contrast, restricted mean survival time can sometimes communicate the
effect more directly than a changing hazard ratio.

# Other Residuals Answer Other Questions

## Martingale residuals and functional form

Let $N_i(t)$ count observed events and let

$$
\widehat M_i(\tau)
=N_i(\tau)-\int_0^\tau Y_i(u)
\exp(x_i^\mathsf{T}\hat\beta)\,d\widehat H_0(u).
$$

This martingale residual is observed minus expected cumulative events. For a
single-event outcome it is bounded above by 1 and is generally skewed. Plotting
it against a continuous predictor omitted from a base model can reveal nonlinear
functional form, but smooth patterns are exploratory and correlated with the
fit. Deviance residuals symmetrize martingale residuals for visual detection of
poorly fit subjects; they do not test PH.

## Score and influence diagnostics

Subject-level score residuals quantify contributions to the coefficient score.
Approximate deletion diagnostics such as dfbeta or dfbetas estimate how much
each coefficient would change if a subject were removed. Large values may signal
data errors, sparse covariate patterns, or legitimate influential biology.
Investigate and report sensitivity; do not delete a subject solely to improve a
plot.

## Cox--Snell residuals and global fit

For an estimated conditional survival distribution, the Cox--Snell residual is

$$
e_i=\widehat H(T_i\mid x_i).
$$

Under a correctly specified continuous-time model, uncensored $e_i$ values have
an exponential reference distribution, with censoring carried through. Comparing
their estimated cumulative hazard with the 45-degree line gives a broad check of
fit. It can miss compensating errors and is not a substitute for covariate-specific
checks.

# A Structured Diagnostic Workflow

1. **Audit design before residuals.** Verify time zero, delayed entry, event
   coding, censoring reasons, competing events, repeated intervals, clusters,
   and information timing for time-dependent covariates.
2. **Inspect support and events.** Tabulate events and subjects at risk over time
   by important covariate patterns. Flag sparse tails and poor overlap.
3. **Check functional forms.** Use subject-matter transformations, martingale
   residual plots, and spline comparisons for continuous predictors.
4. **Assess PH per term.** Plot scaled Schoenfeld residuals with smooths and run
   term-specific and global score tests.
5. **Assess influence.** Examine score residuals, dfbeta summaries, and refits
   excluding or perturbing influential units for transparent sensitivity only.
6. **Check predictions.** Evaluate time-specific calibration, discrimination,
   and optimism with resampling that repeats the complete modeling pipeline.
7. **Fit scientifically plausible alternatives.** Compare conclusions under
   time-varying effects, stratification, alternative endpoint definitions, and
   censoring assumptions.
8. **Report the diagnostic consequences.** State what changed in the estimand,
   coefficients, uncertainty, and biological conclusion.

Running many isolated tests and selecting the model for which all $p$-values
exceed 0.05 is not this workflow. It turns diagnostics into an unreported model
search and gives no guarantee of scientific adequacy.

# Illustrative R Workflow

This non-executed example uses official `survival` package interfaces. Setting
`x = TRUE` retains the design matrix needed efficiently by `cox.zph()`.

```r
library(survival)
library(splines)

fit <- coxph(
  Surv(entry, exit, event) ~ treatment + biomarker + ns(age, 3) + strata(center),
  data = patients,
  ties = "efron",
  x = TRUE
)

ph <- cox.zph(fit, transform = "km", global = TRUE)
print(ph)
plot(ph)

martingale <- residuals(fit, type = "martingale")
deviance   <- residuals(fit, type = "deviance")
influence  <- residuals(fit, type = "dfbeta")
```

The `cox.zph()` table contains a score test for each term and, optionally, a
global test. Its plot estimates a time-varying coefficient; under PH the target
curve is horizontal. A global result cannot identify which term or time region
needs revision, so inspect term-level plots even when the global test is not
significant.

# Bioinformatics Example: A Molecular Subtype Effect

Consider recurrence times for 240 tumor samples classified into molecular
subtypes. The Cox model adjusts for stage, age, and center. The subtype's scaled
Schoenfeld residual curve is near zero early but rises after 18 months.

Before declaring a late biological effect, examine:

- how many independent patients and recurrences remain after 18 months;
- whether follow-up schedules or loss to follow-up differ by subtype;
- whether subtype was measured once at baseline or inferred using outcome-aware
  feature selection;
- whether treatment changes after baseline differ by subtype; and
- whether recurrence and death were combined or treated as competing events.

The patient is the experimental unit. Multiple sections, cells, technical assay
replicates, or sequencing reads from one tumor refine its measurements but do
not create independent event histories. Center-specific assay effects may need
design adjustment; repeated samples may require subject-level clustering and
careful time-dependent coding.

Statistically, a rising residual smooth suggests that a single subtype hazard
ratio is inadequate. Biologically, it may reflect changing disease mechanisms,
treatment selection, depletion of susceptible patients, endpoint heterogeneity,
or technical drift. A time-varying association alone does not identify which
explanation is causal.

# Failure Modes and Sensitivity Analyses

| Diagnostic finding | What it does not prove | Useful next step |
|---|---|---|
| Small PH-test $p$-value | That the covariate has no effect or the whole model is useless | Plot magnitude and shape; fit a plausible time interaction |
| Large PH-test $p$-value | That hazards are proportional | Inspect power, event count, smooths, and alternative transformations |
| Tail departure | A global time-varying biological effect | Show risk-set sizes; truncate only as a prespecified sensitivity analysis |
| Influential subject | A data error | Verify records and support; report deletion sensitivity without automatic exclusion |
| Better residual plot after transformation | A uniquely correct model | Compare scientific interpretability, calibration, and external performance |
| Robust standard errors | Correct PH or functional form | Revise the mean structure; robust covariance addresses uncertainty, not fit |

Important assumptions are partly untestable. Observed data cannot prove that
censoring is conditionally independent, all confounders were measured, the time
origin is biologically comparable, or the study population transports to the
target population. Sensitivity analysis must supplement residual diagnostics.

  and predictive validation.

  organizes conclusions across plausible assumptions and analytic choices.

Schoenfeld residuals are event-time contrasts designed to assess whether Cox
coefficients are constant over time. Their plots and score tests should be read
together and in light of risk-set sizes. Functional form, influence, censoring,
dependence, and calibration require separate checks. When PH fails, the remedy
should follow the scientific estimand—not the desire to make a diagnostic test
nonsignificant.
